newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine mkts seen weathering corruption fallout.
newsitem.headline: Argentine mkts seen weathering corruption fallout.

text.p: The political uncertainty enshrouding Argentina's markets is not likely to have drastic effects, but stocks and debt may underperform if the current climate lingers, say traders and analysts.

Market operators say this week's poor performance by Argentine bonds and stocks has been further complicated by the mixture of U.S. investors booking profits on gains in Bradies this year in addition to jitters around the fall in the Mexican peso.
"Of course this sort of thing doesn't help -- it's all pretty confusing for investors," said Esteban Thomsen, Argentina economist at ING Barings.

Stocks have clocked up losses in excess of two percent this week, on top of last week's 2.5 percent drop in the MerVal blue chip index. The local benchmark dollar-denominated Bocon Previsional bond due 2001 has fallen 1.34 percent since the corruption talk started.
Bonds were lower again Thursday, while stocks nose a bit higher at the open.

The troubles started when former Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo last week accused two ministers of covering up corruption and manipulating judges. Then he reportedly told a judge that President Carlos Menem's chief of staff knew officials had paid bribes to secure a deal between state-run Banco Nacion and U.S. computer giant IBM's local unit.
On Tuesday, the talk led to rumors that a minister was about to resign, which was firmly denied by the government.
"The allegations are potentially very serious," said Frank McGann, first vice-president at Merrill Lynch in Buenos Aires.

But even so, analysts are loath to think there could be any serious negative impact from the accusations. Thomsen of ING says the sniping by Cavallo and government ministers is ultimately just a "soap opera".
Christopher Ecclestone, an analyst at Mexican brokerage house Interacciones commented, "It's not such a problem."
Traders say the bond market's losses have been compounded by U.S. investors, who at the very least have not been encouraged by the corruption talk, booking profits after a year of healthy returns.

Year-to-date, bonds have risen 14 percent. Stocks have just risen seven percent in the same period. But with the recent downturn in bonds, yields have risen, making stocks even less attractive, and exacerbating their slide.

At the same time, stock and bond market players point out that the political corruption talk has been used as an excuse by traders to mark down prices amid very thin volume. Ecclestone suggests the stock market declines "are not a case of actual selling, but buyers waiting for cheaper prices."
The markdown may be disingenuous, some say. "Investors know all emerging markets face corruption," Thomsen noted.

Agustin Etchebarne, senior economist at C&E Consultores says there is probably less corruption in Argentina than in Mexico. Still, in the month-to-date, Argentine bonds are down 2.25 percent compared with a drop of just 0.59 percent in Mexican bonds, according to J.P. Morgan's composite bond indices. Brazil has fallen 1.12 percent in the month.

In fact, McGann of Merrill said all the graft talk could be "very positive" as "the need to improve transparency has come to the fore." He pointed out that the current can of worms was opened by Menem's announcement two weeks ago that he would start cleaning up a customs services corruption scandal, which may have cost state coffers $3 billion.

Also, if Menem's anti-corruption drive boosts the ruling Peronist Party's chances to do well in next year's mid-term Congressional vote it will secure stable government until Menem's term ends in 1999. That will ensure the government moves ahead with its reforms, including the last batch of labor market measures which should reduce employers' costs.
Still, there are risks. If uncertainty lingers, "it could affect the economy," says Etchebarne, because savers will take their deposits out of banks resulting in higher lending rates.
